newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Gold price slump pressures Australia miners.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Gold price slump pressures Australia miners.

text.p: Renewed attacks on the gold price in overnight trading in the United States was putting pressure on Australian mining companies, bullion dealers and analysts said on Friday.
Australian-dollar gold prices are at their lowest in five years and below a growing segment of the industry's average cash operating costs, they said.
Nearly 15 percent, or 43 tonnes, of the nation's gold output was being produced at cash costs of more than A$449 an ounce, analyst Keith Goode of broker Bell Securities Ltd said in a report.
"If the Australian gold price were to fall by 10 percent, this would more than double to 96 tonnes, or approaching 33 percent," Goode said.
The Perth Mint quoted spot gold at A$445.21 an ounce on Friday.
Prospects for a recovery in gold was dealt a further blow as Wall Street remained the focus for investment.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average closed at record levels on Thursday.
"Wall Street is all the rage right now," said a metals dealer.
COMEX April gold ended down US$2.40 at $343.00 an ounce after trading from $346.10 to $342.80, within Wednesday's range. Total estimated volume was 35,000 lots.
In the U.S. bullion market, spot gold ended quoted at $340.75-$341.25, compared to the London afternoon fix of $342.65 and the New York close Wednesday of $342.80-$343.30.
For now, the impact of lower prices on Australian miners may be somewhat muted due to guaranteed forward gold sales at higher prices than the prevailing market.
Due to forward positions, only about 60,000 ounces produced quarterly appears to be under threat of closure down to A$400 an ounce, Goode said.
"Amongst overseas operations where Australian companies have holdings, only about five mines have cash costs above A$400 an ounce and of those about three are contemplating closure," he said.

Consequently, although a third of Australia's gold output would be produced at a loss if the gold price fell another 10 percent, it is not expected to result in the immediate curtailment of the most affected operations, he said.
Most major Australian gold mines use forward sales to operate in the black.
In the fourth quarter of 1996, almost 1.9 million ounces of additional forward positions wwere taken out, Goode said.
"However, the smaller mines do not have the same access," he said.
Nearly 100 tonnes of Australian gold is mined at cash costs of between A$325 and A$400 an ounce, Goode said.
A further 70 tonnes is mined for an average A$205 to A$300 an ounce, he said.
One of the first victims of the sinking gold price has been the Big Rush mine in Western Australia, owned by Werrie Gold Ltd.
Werrie said late last month is was suspending mining at Big Rush as of February 21 in light of the gold price and readily available reserves.
-- James Regan Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
